blocks.text: Brownian motion is the random and irregular motion of molecules in a gas. In 1927, Robert Brown, a botanist observed under microscope that tiny particles of pollens plant were moving around in the liquid randomly. These particles were identified as dust particles. Later, it was proved to be one of the effects of molecular motion.
book_errors: motion of molecules in a gas

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the year 1927 and defines Brownian motion as the motion of molecules in a gas. Robert Brown made his observation in 1827, and Brownian motion is the random motion of small particles suspended in a fluid (here pollen particles in water), caused by collisions with the fluid's molecules.

A molecule changes its path each time it collides with another molecule, so a particle that is hit again and again follows a random, zig-zag path. Each collision transfers momentum and energy (Fig 13.1). Brownian motion is one of the simplest models of randomness. Its main features are:

items: Smaller, lighter particles move faster: the momentum passed to a particle has a larger effect on a lighter particle, so it gains a greater speed.
The speed of the particles is inversely related to the viscosity of the fluid: a fluid of low viscosity gives faster Brownian motion.
Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid, its resistance to flow.
Brownian motion keeps the particles in a fluid in constant motion.

blocks.title: For your information
blocks.text: Albert Einstein explained the movement of pollen particles in a liquid, caused by the molecules, in 1905. In 1908 the French physicist Jean Perrin verified Einstein's explanation by experiment, work that earned him the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics.
